description: Buca Science High School Artificial Intelligence division.
summary: Bufalo Agriculture Intelligence is a web decision-support platform for the “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” challenge. Climate change is making farm planning harder, and the data needed to plan well is scattered across separate NASA portals. BufaloAI brings it together. A farmer draws a field on a satellite map and adds what they know about it, such as soil texture, slope, irrigation, and current rotation. The platform then pulls NASA POWER climate data and satellite vegetation (NDVI) data for that exact location. A GPU-trained XGBoost model forecasts crop vegetation health with uncertainty ranges. It combines this with risk scores and a four-week weather outlook to compare crop rotations, including the farmer’s own. Two AI advisors explain each result in plain language, in Turkish or English, and show confidence levels and information gaps. The tool is meant to support farmer judgement, not replace it. It helps farmers plan water use and crop choices, and reduces the risks of a changing climate.
details:
What it does and how it works

Bufalo Agriculture Intelligence is a browser-based workspace with five connected parts:

  1. Earth atlas and My fields. Users draw a polygon or rectangle on a satellite map, name the field, and fill in “Farmer’s knowledge”: irrigation, soil texture, organic matter, slope, and current rotation. Every value the farmer supplies raises the confidence of later results.
  2. Climate and indicator pages. These show real NASA POWER data for the selected field (temperature, rainfall, humidity, solar radiation, surface soil wetness), plus a “next 4 weeks” outlook that compares expected temperature, rain, frost and hot days to the seasonal normal.
  3. AI intelligence. One click on “Analyse” produces an NDVI forecast, a risk assessment, climate and weather-outlook cards, and rotation suggestions. Each card has a high/medium/low confidence badge, and low-confidence results are visibly flagged. Rotations come from a catalogue, are auto-generated, or are entered by the farmer (“Evaluate my own rotation”), each with estimated damages. Users can also change their priorities and re-score.
  4. Two AI advisors. A Risk & Climate Analyst and a Rotation Advisor write side by side and answer follow-up questions such as “Does growing potatoes here carry risk?”
  5. Crops & rotations. A library of 20 ready-made crops, crop suggestions for the analysed field, and a rotation builder.

Behind this is a pipeline. The backend downloads NASA POWER climate data, MODIS NDVI, and SoilGrids soil data for the field’s location and caches it. A feature layer turns this into model inputs, and XGBoost forecasts NDVI. Risk, weather-outlook, and rotation modules score the result. A language model then turns those numbers into explanations. The language model only explains the numbers. The ML code decides them, so the AI cannot make up figures.

Benefits

  • One place for climate, vegetation, and soil data instead of several portals.
  • Rotation comparison backed by evidence, not guesswork.
  • Honest uncertainty: confidence badges, warnings, a visible disclaimer, and a list of “information gaps” that shows farmers which extra inputs would improve the answer.
  • Plain-language answers, fully in Turkish or English.

Intended impact

We want farmers to plan water use, crop choice, and rotations earlier and with more confidence, and to spot climate and soil risks before they become hard to manage. We also want to show that open NASA data can become a tool a farmer can use without a data science background. The platform supports the farmer’s decision and never replaces it.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Languages and tooling: Python 3.12+ (managed with uv), TypeScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, with session and queue handling, analysis jobs, and a climate API.
  • Frontend: React and Vite.
  • NASA and open data: NASA POWER (climate), MODIS NDVI (vegetation), SoilGrids (soil), Microsoft Planetary Computer.
  • Machine learning: XGBoost on GPU for the NDVI forecast with 10/50/90% quantile uncertainty. The data pipeline uses a PyTorch-style Dataset/DataLoader design. Training happened on a Lenovo Legion laptop with an NVIDIA RTX 5060.
  • AI advisors: Qwen3-8B-FP8 served with vLLM on a dedicated GPU server (RTX 5060 Ti, 16 GB).
  • Infrastructure: Tailscale private network, a Cloudflare named tunnel (spaceapps.nasko.tech), and systemd services with a watchdog and boot check so the site restarts itself.
  • Testing: pytest, with 130+ tests that need no GPU or network.

Creativity

  • Rotation evaluation as the core idea. Instead of only showing weather charts, we compare at least three rotation strategies, including the farmer’s own, and explain the trade-offs.
  • Honesty built in. Uncertainty, missing data, and low confidence are shown to the user, not hidden.
  • Farmer in the loop. The farmer’s own knowledge feeds back into the confidence score.
  • Split of roles. ML computes; the language model explains. This keeps the answers grounded and checkable.
  • Self-hosted AI on modest hardware. The whole stack, advisors included, runs on our own equipment, so it needs no paid AI service.
  • Two languages throughout. Every ML message and advisor answer exists in Turkish and English.

Factors we considered

  • Data limits: NASA POWER has a coarse grid, so we advise users to prefer their own readings when they have them. Satellite data can be delayed, so the system says so instead of guessing.
  • Validation: forecasts are tested on held-out areas and years, not random splits, against persistence and seasonal-climatology baselines.
  • Reliability: failed data sources are recorded as missing, never invented, and the live site restarts itself after failures or reboots.
  • Fairness to the user: the site serves one visitor at a time with a queue, which protects the single GPU and keeps responses reliable.
  • Responsibility: the tool is decision support. It shows evidence and uncertainty and leaves the final call to the farmer.

Note: Project files are located on the official GitHub page. All of the code is open-source, and instructions are provided for setting up the environment.
